summary: Full meshes of MPLS traffic engineering tunnels need a lot of configuration. This document defines IS-IS and OSPF extensions so routers can automatically discover which routers belong to a mesh, which cuts down manual setup. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of telling every router by hand who is in the club, the routers announce their membership and find each other.

questions: automatic discovery of te mesh membership
what is a te mesh group
how do ospf and is-is advertise mesh membership
why automate mpls te full mesh
subtitle: How OSPF and IS-IS routers announce which traffic engineering mesh groups they belong to, so tunnel meshes can be set up automatically.

tldr.problem: A full mesh of MPLS traffic engineering tunnels between N routers needs on the order of N squared tunnels configured by hand, and adding one router means touching every router in the mesh.
tldr.mechanism: Each router advertises its mesh-group numbers, a tail-end address and a tail-end name inside the OSPF Router Information LSA or the IS-IS Router Capability TLV, so other members can discover it.
tldr.outcome: Members of a mesh group can be found automatically through the IGP, which is the first step to automating the tunnel mesh. How the tunnels are then created is left to implementations.

today: RFC 4972 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4970 and RFC 4971.

sections.title: The Cost of a Full TE Mesh
sections.content:
The RFC names two ways to deploy MPLS Traffic Engineering. The strategic approach sets up a full mesh of TE LSPs between a set of LSRs. The tactical approach provisions TE LSPs only on well-identified hot spots, for example to relieve congestion from unexpected traffic growth.

A full mesh is common for bandwidth optimization, bandwidth guarantees or MPLS Fast Reroute, but it needs O(N^2) TE LSPs for N LSRs. Adding one new LSR means configuring N additional TE LSPs on the new router and one new TE LSP on every existing member, for a total of 2*N TE LSPs. The RFC calls this time consuming and risky, since it is prone to misconfiguration.

An automatic mechanism therefore needs a way to discover which LSRs belong to the mesh. That discovery is all this document specifies. The mechanism that dynamically creates the TE LSPs is implementation specific and out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If ten kids must each call every other kid, that is a lot of phone numbers to write down. Adding one more kid means everyone updates their list. It is easier if the kids can find each other on their own.

sections.title: What a TE Mesh-Group Is
sections.content:
A TE mesh-group is a group of LSRs connected by a full mesh of TE LSPs. For each mesh-group membership an LSR announces, it advertises three things:

  • A mesh-group number that identifies the group.
  • A tail-end address, which other LSRs in the same group use as the TE LSP tail-end address.
  • A tail-end name, a display string that makes TE LSPs easier to name.

An LSR may belong to more than one TE mesh-group, and the extensions can signal multiple groups. The RFC also specifies procedures for a member to join and leave a group.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kid says which club number they are in, which phone number to call them on, and a nickname so the calls are easy to label.

sections.title: The TE-MESH-GROUP TLV Formats
sections.content:
The TE-MESH-GROUP TLV advertises the desire of an LSR to join or leave a mesh-group. No sub-TLV is defined for it. Both protocols use two types: 3 carries IPv4 tail-end addresses and 4 carries IPv6 tail-end addresses. The length is variable.

The value holds one or more entries. Each entry has a mesh-group-number, a tail-end IPv4 or IPv6 address, a one-octet name length that gives the length of the tail-end name before padding, and the variable-length tail-end name.

OSPF. The TLV format is the one used by the Traffic Engineering Extensions to OSPF (RFC 3630). It is padded to a four-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the length field. Unrecognized types are ignored, types 32768 to 65535 are reserved for vendor-specific extensions, and other undefined codes are reserved for IANA.

IS-IS. The sub-TLV has one octet for type, one octet for length and a value field, in the same style as the IS-IS TE extensions (RFC 3784). It is carried in the Router CAPABILITY TLV from RFC 4971.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a little form with the same boxes for every club: a club number, a phone number, and a nickname. One version fits short phone numbers and the other fits long ones.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving and Flooding
sections.content:
The TLV rides inside existing capability advertisements, so most procedures are inherited from RFC 4970 (OSPF) and RFC 4971 (IS-IS). The TLV is OPTIONAL. A message MUST NOT include more than one IPv4 instance or more than one IPv6 instance. If one repeats, only the first is processed and later ones SHOULD be silently ignored.

To join or leave a mesh-group, an LSR MUST originate a new LSA (OSPF) or LSP (IS-IS) with the updated TLV. A join adds an entry and a leave removes it, and both can happen in one update. An implementation SHOULD be able to detect any change to a previously received TLV from a given LSR.

In OSPF the TLV travels in a Router Information opaque LSA (opaque type 4, opaque ID 0) for OSPFv2, and in a Router Information LSA for OSPFv3. If the whole mesh-group sits in one area, the TLV MUST be in an area-local LSA. If it spans multiple areas, the TLV MUST be in a routing-domain scope LSA.

In IS-IS, if the scope is limited to a level or area, the sub-TLV MUST NOT be leaked and the S flag of the Router CAPABILITY TLV MUST be cleared. If the scope is the entire routing domain, the sub-TLV MUST be leaked across levels and areas and the S flag MUST be set.
sections.plainLanguage: When a kid joins or leaves a club, they just post an updated sign. If the club is only in one classroom, the sign stays there. If the club spans the whole school, the sign goes everywhere.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC says the new TLVs do not introduce any interoperability issue. A router that does not support the OSPF TE-MESH-GROUP TLV SHOULD silently ignore it, as specified in RFC 2370. An IS-IS router that does not support the sub-TLV SHOULD likewise silently ignore it.

The introduction adds a reason for care: IGPs have relatively tight real-time constraints. The information here is small in volume and relatively stable, since it changes with configuration rather than with dynamic events in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: If a kid does not know about the club signs, they simply walk past them, and nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the function creates no new security issues for OSPF and IS-IS, and points to RFC 2328, RFC 2740 and RFC 1195 for base-protocol security. A fake mesh-group membership from a misconfigured or malicious LSR Y would have no major impact other than overloading the IGP. For another LSR X to set up a TE LSP to Y, the same mesh-group membership must be configured on both, so a fake advertisement could not amplify a denial of service attack.

IANA assigned code-points in both registries: value 3 for the IPv4 TLV and value 4 for the IPv6 TLV, in the OSPF Router Information registry and in the IS-IS Router Capability sub-TLV registry.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone lies about being in a club, nothing happens, because the other kids only call people in clubs they have also joined.
